items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A word or phrase in the question that defines its focus and must be interpreted and addressed"?
items.answer: key term
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of key term.

items.stem: Unpack this Paper 2 question by explaining its command phrase and its key terms: "Discuss the ways in which two works you have studied present conflict between generations."
items.answer: "Conflict between generations" requires parent–child or elder–youth tension and its causes; "ways" asks about authorial methods.
items.markingKey: "Conflict between generations" requires parent–child or elder–youth tension and its causes; "ways" asks about authorial methods. Any suitable studied works may be credited.

items.stem: Distinguish between "In what ways" and "To what extent".
items.answer: "In what ways" asks for an analysis of methods; "to what extent" requires a judgement about degree, with arguments for and against.
items.markingKey: "In what ways" asks for an analysis of methods; "to what extent" requires a judgement about degree, with arguments for and against. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Paper 2 questions refer to specific set texts." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Paper 2 questions are general; students apply them to any two literary works they have studied (but not those used in the IO or HL essay).
items.markingKey: Paper 2 questions are general; students apply them to any two literary works they have studied (but not those used in the IO or HL essay). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Unpack this Paper 2 question by explaining its command phrase and its key terms: "Compare how two works you have studied present a journey, whether literal or metaphorical."
items.answer: "Journey" may be physical travel or inner change; "compare" requires both works to be treated in relation to each other.
items.markingKey: "Journey" may be physical travel or inner change; "compare" requires both works to be treated in relation to each other. Any suitable studied works may be credited.

items.stem: A student claims: "You can answer Paper 2 using a non-literary body of work." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Paper 2 requires two literary works studied in the course.
items.markingKey: Paper 2 requires two literary works studied in the course. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Choosing the right question is the most important decision in Paper 2."
items.answer: Question choice is crucial, but it depends on secure knowledge of the works.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: a well-matched question allows depth; mismatches force irrelevant answers. Arguments against: knowledge of works matters most; good students can adapt to most questions. Supported judgement: Question choice is crucial, but it depends on secure knowledge of the works.

items.stem: Choose a Paper 2-style question and explain in detail how you would interpret its key terms in relation to two works you have studied.
items.answer: Indicative content: key terms defined; command phrase explained; how each work fits; potential comparisons.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: key terms defined; command phrase explained; how each work fits; potential comparisons.

items.stem: How many questions does a student answer in Paper 2?
items.answer: One, chosen from four
items.markingKey: A. Students write one comparative essay.

items.stem: Explain why the key terms of a Paper 2 question must be defined in the essay.
items.answer: General questions use broad terms ("power", "resolution"); defining them in relation to the chosen works shows precise understanding and keeps the essay focused.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: General questions use broad terms ("power", "resolution"); defining them in relation to the chosen works shows precise understanding and keeps the essay focused. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "productive contrast".
items.answer: A difference between works that illuminates both, such as contrasting genres or perspectives
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a difference between works that illuminates both, such as contrasting genres or perspectives. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "The best pairing uses the two works you like most." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The best pairing is the one that answers the question most fully with rich comparison, regardless of preference.
items.markingKey: The best pairing is the one that answers the question most fully with rich comparison, regardless of preference. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why contrasting forms (e.g. a play and a novel) can make a good pairing.
items.answer: Different forms present similar concerns through different methods, giving rich material for comparing authorial choices. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Different forms present similar concerns through different methods, giving rich material for comparing authorial choices. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A Paper 2 question asks about the presentation of power. Explain how you would decide between pairing a tragedy with a dystopian novel or with a poetry collection.
items.answer: Consider which pairing has clear examples of power in both, offers contrasting methods, and lets you analyse authorial choices in depth; justify a choice.
items.markingKey: Consider which pairing has clear examples of power in both, offers contrasting methods, and lets you analyse authorial choices in depth; justify a choice.

items.stem:
Paper 2 question: "How do two works you have studied use structure to create tension?"
Suggest two literary works you could use to answer this question and justify the pairing.
items.answer: Suggested pairing: Gabriel García Márquez's Chronicle of a Death Foretold (in translation) and Shakespeare's Macbeth – both announce or prophesy the outcome early. (any two studied works may be credited if the justification shows a point of comparison and contrast).
items.markingKey: Suggested pairing: Gabriel García Márquez's Chronicle of a Death Foretold (in translation) and Shakespeare's Macbeth – both announce or prophesy the outcome early. items.stem:
Paper 2 question: "Compare how two works you have studied use the perspective of a child or young person."
Suggest two literary works you could use to answer this question and justify the pairing.
items.answer: Suggested pairing: Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird and Marjane Satrapi's Persepolis – child narrators of injustice. (any two studied works may be credited if the justification shows a point of comparison and contrast).
items.markingKey: Suggested pairing: Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird and Marjane Satrapi's Persepolis – child narrators of injustice. (any two studied works may be credited if the justification shows a point of comparison and contrast). Any suitable studied works may be credited.

items.stem:
Paper 2 question: "How do two works you have studied explore the consequences of a single decision?"
Outline three comparative points for an essay answering this question.
items.answer: Example points: the moment of decision; dramatic irony versus metafictional revelation; responsibility and guilt. Evaluate which work makes the reader complicit.
items.markingKey: Example points: the moment of decision; dramatic irony versus metafictional revelation; responsibility and guilt. Evaluate which work makes the reader complicit. Any suitable studied works may be credited.

items.stem: "Students should prepare fixed pairings before the exam." Discuss.
items.answer: Prepare flexible pairings with several points of comparison rather than fixed essays.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: saves time; allows deep preparation of comparisons. Arguments against: questions may not suit prepared pairings; fixed pairings lead to pre-learned essays. Supported judgement: Prepare flexible pairings with several points of comparison rather than fixed essays. Markbands (10 marks): Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem: Briefly explain why students should prepare more than one pairing.
items.answer: Questions vary; flexible pairings let students choose the best fit rather than force a prepared pairing onto an unsuitable question.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Questions vary; flexible pairings let students choose the best fit rather than force a prepared pairing onto an unsuitable question. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a contrast-based pairing and a similarity-based pairing.
items.answer: A similarity-based pairing chooses works with closely shared concerns; a contrast-based pairing chooses works that differ in form or context but meet on the question. Strong essays use both.
items.markingKey: A similarity-based pairing chooses works with closely shared concerns; a contrast-based pairing chooses works that differ in form or context but meet on the question. Strong essays use both. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: For two works you have studied, list four possible Paper 2 question themes they could answer and explain one comparison for each.
items.answer: Indicative content: plausible themes; specific comparison points; awareness of contrasts.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: plausible themes; specific comparison points; awareness of contrasts.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A revision diagram connecting a work's themes to scenes, techniques and quotations"?
items.answer: theme map

items.stem: Explain the difference between memorising quotations and understanding key passages.
items.answer: Memorising quotations provides exact evidence; understanding key passages provides context, structure and methods to discuss even without exact words.
items.markingKey: Memorising quotations provides exact evidence; understanding key passages provides context, structure and methods to discuss even without exact words. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Create a revision plan of five steps for preparing two works for Paper 2 in the final month.
items.answer: For example: reread key passages; build quotation banks by theme; map characters and themes; practise timed plans for past-style questions; write and self-assess full essays.
items.markingKey: For example: reread key passages; build quotation banks by theme; map characters and themes; practise timed plans for past-style questions; write and self-assess full essays.

items.stem: Plan the body of a comparative essay for: "To what extent do two works you have studied end with a sense of resolution?" Give three integrated comparative points.
items.answer: Example points: action versus acceptance; open consequence (what happens to Nora?) versus foreclosed future; the audience's or reader's unresolved discomfort. Judge whether the lack of resolution is the point of each work.
items.markingKey: Example points: action versus acceptance; open consequence (what happens to Nora?) versus foreclosed future; the audience's or reader's unresolved discomfort. Judge whether the lack of resolution is the point of each work. Any suitable studied works may be credited.
